title: How do you decide what price a client should charge?
description: "What price should the client charge?" Setting or changing a price. The structure, the first question to ask, and practice prompts with model answers.
hook: Decide what price to charge by looking from three sides: your costs set the floor, the value to the customer sets the ceiling, and competitors' prices tell you where to land in between. Then test the price against volume, because the goal is the most profit, not the highest price.
body:
When you will use it

Any case about setting or changing a price: pricing a new product, raising prices on an existing one, adding a discount, a free plan or a subscription. The prompt sounds like "What should we charge?" or "Should we raise prices by 10%?"

This is a generate question: "How can we do this?" Lay out the options in buckets that do not overlap, size them, then pick the best. More on the three families of case questions.

Ask this first

What is the goal: profit, market share, or getting customers in fast?

A client chasing share may price low on purpose to win customers, then raise prices later. A client chasing profit wants the price that maximises total contribution. The same product can have different right answers.

The structure

  • Floor: our costs
    • Variable cost per unit (stay above it, unless it is a deliberate loss leader)
    • Fixed costs and investment, recovered over expected volume
  • Ceiling: value to the customer
    • Price of their next best option
    • Extra value we add: savings, time, more revenue for them
  • Reference: the alternatives
    • Competitor prices
    • Substitutes
    • Do we sit above or below them, and why?

Once you have a range, check two things: how volume responds (price elasticity) and the effect on the client's other products. For the three ways to turn this into a number (cost-plus, competitor-based and value-based), see the pricing methods quick tip.

A worked example: should a café raise its price?

An illustrative café sells 1,000 drinks a day at $4.00. The variable cost (milk, coffee, cup) is $1.50 a drink. A rival nearby charges $4.20 for a similar drink. The owner is considering $4.50.

Step 1: check the three sides

Floor: $1.50 variable cost, so either price is well above it. Reference: $4.50 would be 30 cents above the rival, so the café needs a reason customers will pay more, such as better coffee or a better location. Ceiling: for a commuter in a hurry, not walking to the rival may easily be worth more than 30 cents.

Step 2: calculate today's contribution

Contribution per drink: $4.00 − $1.50 = $2.50. Daily contribution: 1,000 × $2.50 = $2,500.

Step 3: find the break-even volume at the new price

At $4.50, contribution per drink is $3.00. To keep $2,500 a day, the café needs $2,500 ÷ $3.00 = 833 drinks. It can lose up to about 16.7% of its volume and still be no worse off.

A useful shortcut: the volume you can afford to lose is the price rise divided by the new contribution per unit. Here, $0.50 ÷ $3.00 = 16.7%.

Step 4: judge whether volume would fall by more than that

This is the real question, and it is more useful than asking whether customers will "accept" the new price. Commuters with little time may barely react; weekend customers comparing with the rival may leave. So test it: raise the price for four weeks at one site and compare its volume with similar sites, by time of day and drink type.

What a strong answer sounds like

"At $4.50 we earn $3 a drink instead of $2.50, so we can lose up to 17% of volume before we are worse off. I doubt commuters will leave in those numbers, but weekend customers might. I'd raise the price on weekday mornings first, test it at one site for a month, and roll it out if volume falls by less than 10%."

A weak answer says "Costs are $1.50, so let's add a markup", using one lens only and never asking how many drinks the café would sell at the new price.

Common mistakes

  • Using only one lens, usually cost-plus, with no volume assumption.
  • Copying competitors without knowing your own costs or how your product differs.
  • Forgetting the break-even volume. It turns a debate into a number you can test.
  • Assuming one response for everyone. Different customers, times and products react differently.
  • Ignoring knock-on effects: rivals' responses, customers switching between your own products, trust.

Practise it

1. The same café considers cutting its price to $3.50 to win customers from the rival. How much must volume rise to break even?

Show the answer

Contribution per drink falls to $3.50 − $1.50 = $2.00. To keep $2,500 a day it needs $2,500 ÷ $2.00 = 1,250 drinks, a 25% increase. Price cuts need large volume gains, and rivals can match them quickly.

2. What price should a company charge for fast EV charging?

Show the answer
  • Cost floor: electricity, grid fees and equipment per kWh; the utilisation needed to break even
  • Customer value: cost of charging at home against on the road; time saved
  • Competitors: rivals' prices and subscriptions; fuel cost per mile as a reference
  • Price structure: per kWh, per minute or subscription; peak and off-peak

Start with cost floor against value ceiling. The trap is copying rivals without knowing your own cost and utilisation.

3. Should a design-software company add a free plan?

Show the answer
  • Acquisition: new users attracted; conversion from free to paid
  • Cannibalisation: paying users moving down; what the free plan leaves out
  • Costs: hosting and support for free users; abuse
  • Competition: rivals' free plans; how customers choose a tool

Start by weighing free-to-paid conversion against paying users who downgrade. The trap is counting sign-ups as success.
